newsitem.title: USA: Florida backs Colombia on drugs certification fight.
newsitem.headline: Florida backs Colombia on drugs certification fight.

text.p: Business groups in Florida said on Wednesday they had formed a lobby to push the U.S. government to reinstate Colombia as a worthy ally in the drugs war.
Jobs and businesses in the United States would suffer if the Clinton administration fails to recertify Colombia this March 1, the Coalition to Certify Colombia said.
It will take part in a forum in Miami on Thursday to present Colombia's case and come up with a strategy to convince Washington of the need to change its mind.
Colombian Vice President Carlos Lemos-Simmonds is due to address the forum and Justice Minister Carlos Eduardo Medellin will also attend.
President Bill Clinton denied certification to Colombia, the world's leading producer of cocaine, under the Narcotics Control Act last March saying it was not doing enough to combat drug trafficking.
The decision meant cuts in aid, other than for anti-narcotics efforts, and affects loan guarantees and trade privileges.
Washington's annual report on countries fighting drugs is due out on March 1.
Clemencia de Tobon, co-ordinator of the 17 organisations in the coalition, said in a statement: "Every day the denial of certification can be seen affecting both Colombians and Americans.

"It affects everyone who purchases fresh-cut flowers, coffee, gasoline and petroleum products and many other consumer products that are exported to the United States by more than 4,000 different companies.

"The denial of certification affects businesses in the United States as well like banks, importers, exporters, freight forwarders, airliners, small businesses, food and beverage vendors and service providers in a broad range of professions."
Exports from Colombia generate more than 15,000 jobs in Florida alone, the statement added.

U.S. sources say Clinton is unlikely to recertify Colombia. Drug fighters were enraged last month when a judge in Cali handed down five-year jail sentences to Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, brothers who head the notorious Cali cocaine cartel. Much tougher sentences had been demanded.

Legislation is pending before Colombia's Congress on stiffer penalties for drug traffickers. And a maritime accord which Colombian officials said will be signed soon stops short of allowing U.S. agents to board suspect vessels within Colombia's 12-mile (19 km) territorial limit.
U.S. drug agents are also alarmed that while the flood of cocaine from Colombia to the United States continues unabated, gangs are increasingly smuggling heroin too.
The coalition said the government was doing all it could to fight the drug gangs and was meeting with success.
Among its members are the Miami chambers of commerce for Colombia, Brazil, Venezuela, Chile and Argentina.
